question: Which blood component is directly responsible for carrying the great majority of oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues?

options.text: White blood cells
Blood plasma
Blood plasma, which carries dissolved gases, nutrients and waste products around the body in solution
Haemoglobin, carried inside the red blood cells

explanation: Haemoglobin, packed inside red blood cells, binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues. Plasma dissolves only a small fraction of the oxygen actually carried; white cells and platelets play no part in oxygen transport.

question: A reduced number of circulating red blood cells (anaemia) affects flight safety mainly because it:

options.text: Raises blood pressure to dangerous levels
Has no measurable effect, since plasma carries most of the oxygen
Lowers the blood's total oxygen-carrying capacity, so tissues (including the brain) receive less oxygen for a given breathing rate
Makes the blood clot more slowly, so oxygen stays in the circulation longer and reaches the tissues more gradually over time, which means the heart rate can be reduced during the flight

explanation: With fewer red cells, there is simply less haemoglobin available to pick up oxygen in the lungs, even though the partial pressure of oxygen in the air is unchanged. This behaves, in effect, like a mild, permanent hypoxic stress.

question: During one cardiac cycle, deoxygenated blood returning from the body passes through the heart in which order?

options.text: Right ventricle, right atrium, then out to the body
Right atrium, right ventricle, then out to the lungs
Left atrium, left ventricle, then out to the lungs through the pulmonary artery, before returning to the systemic circulation
Left atrium, left ventricle, then out to the lungs

explanation: Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium, is pumped into the right ventricle, and is then sent to the lungs through the pulmonary artery to be oxygenated, before returning to the left side of the heart for distribution to the body.

question: Most of the carbon dioxide produced by the body's tissues is carried back to the lungs:

options.text: Dissolved in the plasma as bicarbonate ions, not directly bound to haemoglobin
As a gas trapped inside white blood cells
Bound to haemoglobin in exactly the same way as oxygen, using the same binding site
It is not transported at all; it diffuses directly through the skin

explanation: The majority of CO2 is converted to bicarbonate and carried dissolved in the plasma; only a smaller fraction is carried bound to haemoglobin (at a different site from oxygen) or dissolved directly as gas.

question: The pulmonary circulation is the part of the circulatory system that:

options.text: Carries blood between the heart and the rest of the body
Carries blood only within the brain
Is active only during exercise, when the heart rate rises and extra blood is sent to the working muscles of the limbs
Carries blood between the heart and the lungs for gas exchange

explanation: The circulatory system is split into two loops: the pulmonary circulation, moving blood to and from the lungs for gas exchange, and the systemic circulation, distributing oxygenated blood to and from the rest of the body.

question: Atherosclerosis — the narrowing of arteries by fatty deposits — is dangerous mainly because it:

options.text: Directly reduces the number of red blood cells produced by the bone marrow, leaving the blood with less capacity to carry oxygen
Increases the lungs' ability to absorb oxygen
Directly reduces the number of red blood cells produced
Restricts blood flow to tissues such as the heart muscle, and can lead to a blockage that causes a heart attack

explanation: Narrowed, fatty-deposit-laden arteries restrict blood supply to the tissue they feed. When a coronary artery supplying the heart muscle itself becomes blocked, the result is a heart attack (myocardial infarction).

question: Which combination below best represents recognized, modifiable risk factors for coronary heart disease?

options.text: Wearing corrective lenses, having a high body temperature and taking a short course of routine antibiotics during the year
Blood group, eye colour and height
Smoking, a high-fat diet, lack of exercise, obesity and chronic stress
Having had a childhood vaccination

explanation: Smoking, poor diet, inactivity, obesity and chronic stress are all modifiable lifestyle factors that raise the risk of coronary heart disease — unlike fixed factors such as age, sex or family history, these can actually be changed.

question: Carbon monoxide is especially dangerous to aircrew because it:

options.text: Is easily detected by its strong smell before any symptoms appear, so a pilot can notice it early in the cabin and act before feeling any effect at all
Binds to haemoglobin far more readily than oxygen does, so even a small concentration can significantly cut the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity
Has no effect on haemoglobin and only irritates the lungs directly
Is only found at ground level and cannot reach cruising altitude

explanation: Carbon monoxide has a far greater affinity for haemoglobin than oxygen does, so it occupies the binding sites oxygen would otherwise use, cutting the blood's effective oxygen-carrying capacity even at low concentrations. It is colourless and odourless, so it gives no warning on its own.

question: A pilot with carbon monoxide bound to a portion of their haemoglobin, then exposed to reduced cabin pressure at altitude, will show symptoms of hypoxia:

options.text: At a higher altitude than normal, because carbon monoxide improves cell respiration
At exactly the same altitude, since carbon monoxide has no effect once in flight
Only after landing, never while still airborne, because the symptoms only develop once the aircraft has returned to ground level and the pressure has stabilised
At a lower altitude than a pilot with normal haemoglobin, because the carbon monoxide has already reduced the oxygen-carrying capacity available

explanation: Carbon monoxide exposure (for example from a faulty exhaust heater, or from smoking before flight) effectively adds to the hypoxic stress of altitude, because the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity is already reduced before the aircraft climbs at all.

question: Beyond the effects of carbon monoxide, smoking also raises cardiovascular risk because nicotine:

options.text: Has no cardiovascular effect at all, since its only action is on the lungs and the airway and does not reach the circulation
Constricts blood vessels and raises heart rate and blood pressure
Dilates blood vessels, lowering blood pressure
Increases the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood

explanation: Nicotine is a vasoconstrictor and a stimulant: it narrows blood vessels and increases both heart rate and blood pressure, adding a cardiovascular workload on top of the oxygen-carrying penalty from carbon monoxide.

question: Blood pressure is usually expressed as two numbers, for example 120/80. The first (higher) number is:

options.text: Pressure measured only in the pulmonary circulation, through the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs
An average of the pressure over the full cardiac cycle
Systolic pressure, measured while the heart is contracting
Diastolic pressure, measured while the heart is relaxed

explanation: Systolic pressure is the peak pressure generated while the ventricles contract and eject blood; diastolic pressure, the lower of the two, is the pressure remaining in the arteries while the heart relaxes between beats.

question: Pressoreceptors (baroreceptors) in the walls of major arteries help maintain stable blood pressure by:

options.text: Acting only during sleep, switching off during waking hours so that blood pressure is left entirely to the kidneys and hormones
Acting only during sleep, switching off during waking hours
Detecting changes in arterial pressure and triggering reflex adjustments to heart rate and vessel diameter
Producing red blood cells in response to low pressure

explanation: Baroreceptors sense stretch in the artery wall caused by pressure changes and signal the nervous system to adjust heart rate and vessel tone, which is what keeps blood pressure relatively stable as posture and activity change.

question: A pilot who stands up abruptly after sitting for a long period may briefly feel light-headed. This is best explained by:

options.text: A short delay before the baroreceptor reflex corrects the drop in blood pressure to the brain caused by gravity pooling blood in the lower body
An immediate rise in blood oxygen content
A permanent change in heart structure, caused by a long period of inactivity, which alters the shape and wall thickness of the heart chambers over time
A sudden increase in red blood cell production

explanation: Standing suddenly shifts blood toward the legs under gravity, briefly reducing blood pressure to the brain. The baroreceptor reflex normally compensates within seconds; a momentary lag is what produces the light-headed sensation (orthostatic hypotension).

question: Why are aircrew typically advised against flying duties for a short period after donating blood?

options.text: Donation temporarily reduces blood volume and red cell count, lowering the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity while the body replaces what was lost
Donated blood is immediately replaced in full within minutes
It has no physiological effect; the restriction exists only for administrative reasons
Donated blood is immediately replaced in full within minutes by the body, so there is no period of reduced capacity to be concerned about at all after donating

explanation: A donation removes a measurable volume of blood and red cells. The body takes time to restore both, so until it does, the oxygen-carrying capacity available to the donor is reduced — exactly the kind of reserve a pilot needs when combined with altitude.

question: A pulmonary embolism relevant to long-haul flying is most directly caused by:

options.text: A build-up of carbon dioxide in the cabin air supply
An allergic reaction to cabin air filtration, which causes the airways to narrow and the blood vessels in the lungs to swell during the flight
An allergic reaction to cabin air filtration
A blood clot, often formed in a leg vein during prolonged immobility, travelling to and blocking a blood vessel in the lungs

explanation: Sitting still for long periods promotes sluggish blood flow in the legs, encouraging a deep vein thrombosis. If part of that clot breaks free, it can travel through the venous system and lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolism, which can be life-threatening.

question: Which in-flight habit most directly reduces the risk of deep vein thrombosis on a long flight?

options.text: Periodically moving the legs and ankles, and walking the cabin when able, to keep venous blood from pooling
Drinking several alcoholic drinks to help sleep through the flight
Remaining completely motionless to conserve energy
Wearing tight footwear to compress the lower leg, since the pressure is believed to push blood back toward the heart during the flight

explanation: Calf and ankle movement activates the muscle pump that helps return venous blood to the heart. Remaining still for hours, or using alcohol (which promotes dehydration and immobility), both work against this and raise clot risk.

question: A positive family history of coronary heart disease is best understood, in the context of personal risk, as:

options.text: A guarantee that heart disease will occur regardless of lifestyle
A non-modifiable factor that raises personal risk, making the modifiable factors (diet, exercise, smoking) even more important to control
A factor that can be changed through diet alone, so that once diet is corrected the inherited element of the risk is removed entirely, with no further action needed
Irrelevant, since heart disease is purely a matter of lifestyle

explanation: Family history cannot be changed, but it does raise baseline risk. That makes managing the risk factors that can be changed — weight, exercise, smoking, diet — proportionately more important for someone who carries that history.

question: The heart's own blood supply is delivered through:

options.text: Diffusion directly from the blood passing through its own chambers
The pulmonary veins, which also oxygenate the ventricles directly
The coronary arteries, which branch off the aorta to feed the heart muscle itself
The pulmonary veins, which also oxygenate the ventricles directly by delivering blood from the lungs straight into the heart chambers

explanation: The heart muscle is itself a tissue that needs its own blood supply, delivered by the coronary arteries branching from the aorta — it is not nourished simply by the blood passing through its chambers.

question: Chronic high blood pressure (hypertension) increases cardiovascular risk mainly by:

options.text: Having no long-term effect if the person feels no symptoms
Having no long-term effect if the person feels no symptoms, since damage to the arteries is always accompanied by noticeable pain
Forcing the heart to work harder over time and accelerating damage to artery walls
Directly increasing the number of red blood cells produced

explanation: Sustained high pressure makes the heart work against greater resistance and promotes damage to the artery lining, both of which accelerate the processes that lead to heart attack and stroke — this proceeds silently, which is exactly why it is dangerous even without symptoms.

question: Platelets (thrombocytes) in the blood are primarily responsible for:

options.text: Fighting infection by carrying white blood cells and antibodies to sites where bacteria or viruses have entered the body
Carrying oxygen to the tissues
Initiating clotting to stop bleeding when a blood vessel is damaged
Regulating body temperature

explanation: Platelets clump together and trigger the clotting cascade at a site of injury. Oxygen carriage is haemoglobin's job and infection defence is the white blood cells' job — a reminder that blood's functions are divided among specialised components.

question: A heavy smoker who has not smoked for several hours before a flight, compared with a non-smoker, will generally:

options.text: Still carry a measurably higher level of carboxyhaemoglobin and so tolerate altitude hypoxia slightly less well, since carbon monoxide clears the body only gradually
Have a higher oxygen-carrying capacity than a non-smoker, because nicotine stimulates the bone marrow to produce extra red blood cells, which then circulate throughout the body for the whole day
Have a higher oxygen-carrying capacity than a non-smoker
Have exactly the same oxygen-carrying capacity, since the effect of smoking is immediate and wears off completely within minutes

explanation: Carbon monoxide bound to haemoglobin is cleared slowly — over several hours, not minutes — so a smoker can carry a meaningful handicap into a flight even without smoking immediately beforehand, reducing their margin against hypoxia at altitude.

question: If the heart's pumping efficiency falls (for example, in heart failure), the most direct consequence for human performance in flight is:

options.text: No effect, since the lungs alone determine oxygen delivery
An improvement in reaction time, because a slower heart rate lets the brain process more information between each beat and react faster
An automatic increase in haemoglobin concentration that fully compensates
Reduced delivery of oxygenated blood to tissues including the brain, which can mimic or worsen the effects of hypoxia

explanation: Oxygen delivery depends on both adequate oxygen uptake in the lungs and adequate pumping by the heart to circulate it. A weaker pump reduces delivery to tissue even if the lungs themselves are working normally, producing effects that can resemble hypoxia.
